newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Expected S.Africa rate cut seen boosting stocks.
newsitem.headline: Expected S.Africa rate cut seen boosting stocks.

text.p: An expected cut in South African interest rates should bolster interest-sensitive stocks and create significant buying opportunities, Oasis Asset Management managing director Adam Ebrahim said on Wednesday.
Presenting his new company to the media in Cape Town, Ebrahim said his investment team would focus on picking stocks, rather than on indices or markets.

"Essentially, we're stock-pickers. But if I look at the market as a whole, I don't believe that in a declining interest rate environment there is any substantial downward adjustment pending," he said.
Ebrahim echoed the market expectation of a cut soon in the central Reserve Bank's key 17 percent interest rate, which has remained unchanged for eight months.
A Reuters poll of more than 20 economists showed in June that most expect at least a one percentage point cut this year and at least two percentage points by the end of the first quarter of 1998.
Hopes for an imminent cut were dampened by worse than expected credit extension figures earlier this week, but bolstered by better than expected inflation figures.
"If interest rates come down, there should be substantial buying opportunities amongst interest-sensitive stocks. Some of them are pretty attractively priced," Ebrahim said.

"In the last two weeks, we have seen substantial upticks in those types of shares, barring the financials. We're talking about the GDFI (gross domestic fixed investment) type stocks and the credit retailers.
"Also some of the exporters and the chemical sector look good to me right now," he said.
Ebrahim said banks were substantially overpriced, adding: "If you look at the ratings, they've never been more expensive and you really not going to want to be buying there."
Ebrahim and director James Frater presented their Oasis Asset Management company to the media on Wednesday pending a formal public launch next week.
"We're looking mainly at pension and retirement funds and high net-worth individuals," said Frater.
"In the longer term, we will have a product that is accessible to everyone," he said.
He said the company currently managed assets of 100 million rand ($21.8 million).
